newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek village bucks apathy trend, refuses to vote.
newsitem.headline: Greek village bucks apathy trend, refuses to vote.

text.p: Unprecedented excitement about Sunday's national election has gripped the impoverished villagers of this western Greek backwater.

Contrary to the widespread apathy that has pervaded the election campaign, the people of Strongylovouni are passionate about it -- passionate in refusing to cast their mandatory vote, risking imprisonment.
"We are all determined not to vote," village mayor Ilias Kossovas told Reuters. "We know the penalties but we feel politicians have cheated us. We are forgotten."
This furious reaction was prompted by the closure of one of the village's two elementary schools, which are 3.5 km (two miles) apart and serve two distant clusters of farming homes.

"Six-year-olds going to school for the first time can't walk this distance and, even if transport is provided, I don't trust anyone driving my kids on these rugged roads in the winter," said Haroula Borbotsialou, 35, a mother of four.

But, most importantly, people here feel closing down the school is tantamount to killing their village, perched among rolling hills 35 km (20 miles) northwest of the town of Messolongi, where the English poet Lord Byron died.
"Village life centres around the church and the school. If we close these, we shut down the village," Borbotsialou said.

Refusing to vote is no simple affair in Greece, where it carries a jail sentence of between a month and a year. Offenders are also banned from getting a passport, a driver's licence or opening a business.
But Strongylovouni's 340 inhabitants say they are unanimous and determined not to cast their ballots for anyone.

The village subsists on tobacco, cotton and corn farming, products restricted by European Union quotas. Like most farming villages in Greece, it has seen its economy shrink and its youth leave to seek a better life in the big cities.
Rusting farm machinery lies along the dirt roads criss-crossing old stone houses, makeshift huts and animal pens set among oaks and olive trees.
The one-room school which 17 children are scheduled to attend this year has a concrete floor and is heated by a wood stove.
"Politicians come when they need our vote, then they turn their backs on us," said Theodora Davatzi, 60, a grandmother.
"I have eyes but I am blind. I don't know how to read and write because we had the German occupation when I was a child. These children must have education," she added.
The mayor proudly points out that in 1965 the village boasted 100 elementary school students.
"Now we have 20 eligible bachelors and no women for them. The girls all leave to go to bigger towns. We'll have to advertise in Albania for brides," he said.
Villio Kosma, 18, who is preparing for university entrance exams, explains that the hardships of agricultural life and stifling small-town mentalities are driving girls away.
"I love this village but it has nothing to offer," she said. "Life here is hard and I want to make my life in a place where you can have fun and nobody cares what you do."

Despite generous handouts by the socialists that breathed new life into the countryside in the 1980s, Greece's agricultural sector has also fallen victim to an austerity aimed at cutting deficits and inflation.

EU subsidies have been drastically cut since the years of the late prime minister Andreas Papandreou, whose free-spending policies endeared him to the provinces and assured him three election victories.
His passionate oratory and defiance of Greece's big-power Western allies made Papandreou hugely popular, especially in villages like this all over Greece.
"The socialist handouts were like a rainstorm that came and passed," Borbotsialou said.

Papandreou's socialist successor as prime minister, Costas Simitis, a bland technocrat who promises more economic austerity to keep in line with EU requirements, has not inspired these people who see their incomes being reduced year by year.
Simitis's conservative opponent, Miltiadis Evert, has also failed to convince them his generous campaign promises will become reality after the election.
Public opinion polls show the two running neck-and-neck, while voter interest appears to be at a record low for the usually politically passionate Greeks.
The mood of indifference is evident here. There are none of the usual slogans painted alongside country roads and hardly any posters of candidates stuck on walls and electricity poles.
Asked about the single poster of a man in a blue suit hung outside the Strongylovouni coffee house, the villagers laugh.
"That's not a politician. That's a bouzouki singer performing in the nearby town tonight," the proprietor said.
